conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the surgery team. You’re back from Interventional Radiology after the gastrostomy tube placement. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little groggy. My belly hurts where the tube is. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—some soreness around the tube site is expected for the first few days. We’ll keep an eye on it and treat the pain with oral medication as you’re able to take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did everything go okay with the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It went smoothly. The report says it was an uncomplicated, fluoroscopy-guided placement, and the tube is positioned in the gastric remnant where we want it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So this is to get me off the TPN, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The goal is to transition from parenteral nutrition through the PICC to enteral nutrition through the G-tube, since feeding the gut is generally safer and better long-term when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous because eating has been so hard. The nausea and dry heaves are still happening most days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. The tube feeds let us give nutrition in a controlled way even when solid food is difficult. We’ll start gently—first clear liquids by mouth today if you feel up to it, and we’ll start tube feeds after the first 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why do we have to wait 24 hours to use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after placement, we give the tract time to settle and we monitor for any early issues like bleeding, worsening pain, or signs of infection. If everything stays stable, we begin feeds and advance stepwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I drink water now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—clear liquids are fine. Start slow. If you feel nausea, let us know and we can adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tight when I move. Am I allowed to get up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we want you to. We’ll help you the first time. Walking reduces the risk of blood clots and helps your lungs. You’ll also have compression boots and you’ll get heparin shots to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed the PICC line is still there. Are we keeping it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’ll keep it while we’re transitioning. Once you’re tolerating tube feeds at goal, we can remove the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is not terrible right now, but I’m scared it’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll monitor closely. You’re continuing your nortriptyline at bedtime, and we’ll keep your acid suppression as well. The hope is that steady nutrition through the tube will also help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what the nortriptyline is for? GI mentioned something about cyclic vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI raised concern for possible cyclical vomiting syndrome, and nortriptyline is sometimes used to reduce the frequency and severity of those nausea/vomiting cycles. You mentioned you’ve had some improvement since starting it, even though symptoms aren’t fully gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The tube site stings. How will I know if it’s infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. Mild soreness is normal. Concerning signs are increasing redness, swelling, warmth, foul odor, yellow or bloody drainage, fever, or worsening pain instead of gradual improvement. We’ll teach you how to check it daily at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night? Any vomiting or fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. I had some nausea but no throwing up. The pain is mostly at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Your vitals have been stable. Today we’ll start tube feeds and advance as tolerated. We’ll also keep tracking your labs and hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of tube feeding is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The plan is a formula called Replete with Fiber. We’ll work up to a goal rate and then cycle it over 12 hours, so it can run overnight at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—tube feeds don’t prevent you from eating by mouth. We’ll advance your oral diet as you tolerate it. The tube is there to make sure you get enough nutrition even if your intake is limited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the feeds will make me nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea increases, we can slow the rate, pause, or adjust the schedule. We’ll start gradually and see how your body responds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the tube feeds. How are you feeling so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surprisingly okay. A little full, but not like the dry heaves I get with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep advancing toward the goal rate as long as you’re comfortable and your abdomen stays soft without worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with this tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but avoid soaking it—no baths, hot tubs, or swimming. Clean the area gently with warm soapy water and keep it dry otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the cap? Do I keep it capped when it’s not running?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. When it’s not in use, you can cap the outside opening and secure the tube to your abdomen with tape so it doesn’t tug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is dry. Do I need extra water with the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your home plan includes free-water flushes—150 mL three times a day through the tube. You can also drink fluids by mouth as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re at the goal tube feed rate now. How did you do overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually slept. I had less nausea than usual. The site is still sore but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your pain control sounds appropriate, and it’s encouraging that nausea is improving. We can also advance you to a regular diet by mouth today, as tolerated, while continuing the tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Regular diet? Even with my bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As tolerated—small amounts, slow, and stop if you feel symptoms. The tube feeds are the main nutrition right now; the oral diet is to see what you can comfortably take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do you take out the PICC? I’m worried about infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now that you’re tolerating tube feeds at goal, we can remove the PICC today. That reduces infection risk and means you won’t need IV nutrition at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go home with the pump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home with services and a Zevex Infinity pump. The feeds will run at 110 mL per hour for 12 hours, and you’ll do the water flushes three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I get constipated from the pain medicine or the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending docusate liquid to use as needed for constipation. Also keep walking and stay hydrated—both help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared I’ll mess up the tube at home. What if it gets pulled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common worry. Keep it secured to your abdomen, avoid tugging, and be careful with clothing and seatbelts. If it dislodges or you have sudden severe pain, fever, or vomiting you can’t control, call us or come to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your home medications unless we specifically told you otherwise. You’ll continue aripiprazole, citalopram, lamotrigine, lorazepam, nortriptyline at bedtime, and temazepam as needed. Your pantoprazole will be a 40 mg tablet once daily now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain, just the liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—use it as needed. Don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it, and let us know if pain is worsening instead of improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me call right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call for fever over 101.5, severe or worsening abdominal pain, increasing redness or drainage at the tube site, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, signs of dehydration like dizziness when standing, or any blood or black material in vomit or stool. Otherwise, keep the site clean and dry, walk several times a day, and follow up as arranged.
